results.message: What are your sources for what you believe about baptism?

voice_event.speaker: lpc
voice_event.text:
We baptized infants before the eighth day, and we taught adults the creed before bringing them to the water. Both came from the practice handed down to us. For the infants, Cyprian and sixty-six bishops met in council and wrote to Fidus. He had wanted to wait. They gave their reason. The newborn has not sinned by his own act, but he carries the contagion of the old death from Adam. So Cyprian's council wrote: “Even the greatest sinners, who had sinned much against God, are granted forgiveness of sins when they later believe. No one is kept from baptism and grace. How much more, then, should we shrink from keeping back an infant! Being newly born, he has not sinned, except in one way. Born in the flesh as Adam’s child, he caught the infection of the ancient death at his very first birth. For this very reason he comes the more easily to receive the forgiveness of sins. What is forgiven him is not his own sins, but the sins of another.”

Augustine went to the hard end of what that means. The mildest punishment of all is still punishment. For adults, we taught them first. Augustine wrote a guide to catechesis, teaching the creed before the washing. We also answered twice, in opposite ways, whether a baptism given outside our one church counts at all. Cyprian said it counts for nothing. Augustine said it is truly given but does no good there. Augustine argued at length that Cyprian's ruling was wrong. He never put Cyprian outside our communion.

glosses.plain_meaning: For us, grace is the insistence that no effort of ours is enough on its own. Any good a person does was given to them before they did it.
glosses.quick_meaning: For us, grace means this: no one's own effort is ever enough. Whatever good a person does was given to them first.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern listener is likely to hear grace as a warm general benevolence, or as 'grace under pressure,' or as a denominational shibboleth they may already have an opinion about, and to hear our anti-Pelagian position as harsh determinism. We mean a specific and contested claim about the priority of divine action over human capacity, argued against a named opponent over roughly a decade, with direct consequences for how a congregation is taught, how failure is handled, and what a pastor can reasonably ask of anyone.
false_friend: a warm general benevolence, or 'grace under pressure,' with no specific claim about the priority of divine action over human capacity
a denominational shibboleth in a Protestant-Catholic argument the participant may already hold an opinion about

glosses.plain_meaning: You are taught before you are washed. We tell you what you are joining before you join it. You say the creed back, and then we baptize you.
glosses.quick_meaning: For us, catechesis means teaching people before they are baptized. We teach them the creed, and the basics of belief, before the water, not after it.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern listener may hear a children's catechism -- rote question-and-answer, memorized young, faintly dry. Catechesis itself was built around adult instruction, before baptism, of people making a consequential change of standing. It was taken seriously enough that a working manual for instructors exists. Baptism was not adult-only, though. Augustine writes plainly that those baptized into Christ's own death include "not adults only, but infants as well." That is a different question from who received instruction, and this term does not answer it by itself.
false_friend: a children's catechism -- rote question-and-answer, memorized young, faintly dry

glosses.plain_meaning: For us, communion is a formal standing within the one body. You can lose it, and be given it back. At the council of 256, Cyprian said no one would be put out of it for thinking differently.
glosses.quick_meaning: For us, communion is a real standing inside the one body. You can lose it, and be given it back. Cyprian held that it should survive sharp disagreement.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern listener is likely to hear either a specific liturgical rite -- going up to receive -- or a general warmth of fellowship, and the second makes disagreement look like a failure of communion. We mean a formal, structural status of standing within the body, with public consequences, that, on Cyprian's own principle, disagreement should not dissolve. Disagreement is expected among us; what would break communion is not arguing but separating.
false_friend: a specific liturgical rite alone, going up to receive, with no broader sense of standing attached
a general warmth of fellowship and mutual good feeling, so that any real disagreement looks like a failure of it

names.name: Thascius Caecilius Cyprianus, bishop of Carthage (248/249-258)

figures_used.bridge_line: Our bishop, chosen while still new to the faith, over his own reluctance. During a plague he taught us to love even our enemies. He was put to death under Valerian.

dates.display: a trained rhetorician who turned from a public career to Christian life, converted c. 246; ordained and elected bishop of Carthage between roughly July 248 and April 249 by the acclamation of the Carthaginian people, over the recorded opposition of five presbyters, while still newly baptised, as his deacon Pontius tells it; banished to Curubis under the Valerianic persecution; executed under the emperor Valerian in 258

names.name: Augustinius of Hippo Regius, presbyter 391, bishop 395/396-430

figures_used.bridge_line: Our bishop at Hippo. The people seized him and brought him to be made a presbyter while he wept. Later they pressed him into the bishop's office over his own refusal. He spent his last days weeping over psalms of penitence, while an army lay outside the walls.

dates.display: converted 386, baptised 387; seized by the congregation at Hippo and ordained presbyter against his own wishes in 391, weeping through it (Possidius, Vita IV); designated coadjutor and consecrated bishop of Hippo by Megalius, primate of Numidia, in 395/396, again amid popular acclamation (Possidius, Vita VIII); died 430, during the Vandal siege of Hippo

confidence.divergence_note: The entire evidentiary base for this term is one voice (Augustine) within one evidence stream (the anti-Pelagian corpus), flagged at generation rather than discovered afterwards (Author-Gravity-Risk: Yes). No Pelagian first-person answer survives in our own record. This term also carries a live scholarly contest, kept on its own axis, independent of this historical-fact rating. The contest type is Relationship to present-day traditions, secondarily Meaning. It runs over how the historical position stands to the way living traditions use the word now, including later appropriations and the Catholic-Protestant disagreements that ran through them, and over the modern reassessment of whether the position Augustine argued against is the one Pelagius held. The entry does not present the anti-Pelagian position as the settled meaning of the word across Christian history, and it does not characterize Pelagius.

The text field is the ANF English as printed. An ANF editor's bracketed note, with verses by George Canning, sits inside section 5 after 'according to Adam,'. It is not Cyprian's. It is not part of the passage and is left out.

elements.surface: “Even the greatest sinners, who had sinned much against God, are granted forgiveness of sins when they later believe. No one is kept from baptism and grace. How much more, then, should we shrink from keeping back an infant! Being newly born, he has not sinned, except in one way. Born in the flesh as Adam’s child, he caught the infection of the ancient death at his very first birth. For this very reason he comes the more easily to receive the forgiveness of sins. What is forgiven him is not his own sins, but the sins of another.”

confidence.divergence_note: Attested through dedicated treatises rather than raw recurrence of a headword -- a different, but not weaker, kind of ground: a manual written to instruct instructors is stronger evidence of a practice's own centrality than word-frequency alone would be.
